description: Jisk'a Iru Muqu is a pre-Columbian open-air site in the Aymara community of Jachacachi, 54 km southeast of Puno, Peru, at 3,890 m elevation in the Lake Titicaca Basin. Occupied from c. 3400-1600 BCE (Late Archaic to Early Formative), it was the first Archaic open-air site excavated in the Titicaca Basin, discovered by Mark Aldenderfer in 1994. Excavations (1995, 1999-2004) by UC Santa Barbara recovered obsidian tools, a gold necklace, and early domestic architecture showing reduced residential mobility. The site provides critical evidence for the transition from mobile foraging to settled village life in the south-central Andes.

card_description: A cave occupied 70,000 years ago where seven Neanderthals were buried, including infants and a fetus. One of the strongest cases for Neanderthal burial rituals.
description: A major Palaeolithic rock shelter in Savignac-de-Miremont, Dordogne, France, where Neanderthal fossils were discovered between 1909 and 1921. Eight individuals were found intentionally buried at the site, including a man, a woman, children, an infant, and newborns, dating to approximately 50,000 years ago. The adult male La Ferrassie 1 preserves the largest and most complete Neanderthal skull ever found. One child's grave contained a skull covered by a limestone slab with markings on its underside, suggesting ritualistic behavior. The site provided key evidence for Neanderthal burial practices and is associated with Middle Palaeolithic Mousterian stone tools.

card_description: A 74 km road through Norfolk and Suffolk follows a Roman-era route that writers have argued predates Roman arrival. Its name comes from the medieval word pedder — meaning a travelling merchant.
description: Peddars Way is a 74 km (46 mi) long-distance path following a Roman road from Knettishall Heath in Suffolk to Holme-next-the-Sea in Norfolk. Its remarkably straight alignment reflects Roman military engineering, though it may predate the Romans as a prehistoric trackway linked to the Icknield Way. The route passes Castle Acre with its medieval priory and Norman castle earthworks, and intersected Roman installations including a fort at Brettenham and the Saxon Shore fort at Brancaster. Today it forms part of the Peddars Way and Norfolk Coast Path National Trail.

description: Xelha (meaning 'water inlet' in Mayan) is an archaeological site on the Caribbean coast of Quintana Roo, Mexico, initially settled around 600 BC. The site features the Casa de los Pajaros with murals showing Teotihuacan influence, and the Jaguar Group with vivid blue and red painted murals -- among the most outstanding Maya paintings on the Caribbean coast. In 1527, conquistador Francisco de Montejo established a short-lived Spanish settlement here called 'Salamanca de Xelha'.

card_description: The smallest Old Kingdom pyramid, from the 24th century BC. Its walls hold the Pyramid Texts — the oldest religious writings on Earth.
description: The Pyramid of Unas is a smooth-sided pyramid built in the 24th century BC for Pharaoh Unas, the ninth and final king of Egypt's Fifth Dynasty[1]. Located in North Saqqara between the complexes of Sekhemket and Djoser, it is the smallest Old Kingdom pyramid[1]. Despite its modest size, it holds immense historical significance as the first pyramid to contain Pyramid Texts—spells for the king's afterlife incised into the walls of its subterranean chambers[1]. This innovation initiated a tradition that continued in subsequent royal pyramids through the end of the Old Kingdom and evolved into the Coffin Texts of the Middle Kingdom, which later formed the basis of the Book of the Dead[1].

description_citations.claim: The pyramid of Unas is the funerary monument built for the Egyptian pharaoh Unas, the ninth and final king of the Fifth Dynasty, in the 24th century BC. Inscribed for the first time in Unas's pyramid, the tradition of these funerary texts carried on in the pyramids of subsequent rulers through to the end of the Old Kingdom, and into the Middle Kingdom through the Coffin Texts that form the basis of the Book of the Dead.

description: Baumann's Cave (Baumannshohle) in Rubeland, Harz district, is Germany's oldest show cave, formed in Devonian limestone dating back over 350 million years. The cave has been used by humans since the Stone Age, with finds of bones, pottery shards, and stone tools attesting to early occupation. Open to the public with guided tours since 1649 when Valentin Wagner became its first cave guide, it was also recognized as the first legally protected natural monument in Germany. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe visited the cave three times between 1777 and 1784, lending his name to the Goethesaal, the cave's largest chamber, which now serves as a unique underground venue for theatre performances and concerts.

Later reanalysis revealed medieval glass beads with chemical compositions matching those from nearby Dunadd, suggesting continued use of the site into the early medieval period.

card_description: 4th-7th century AD Iron Age broch on the island of Barra with two distinct occupation phases centuries apart. Dun Cuier is considered complex and controversial — one of Scotland's most debated brochs.
description: Dun Cuier is a broch-like galleried dun on the island of Barra in the Outer Hebrides, perched on a rocky summit about 46 metres above sea level. The structure measures 14.5 metres in overall diameter with walls approximately 5 metres thick, featuring a narrow gallery running around most of the circuit and a scarcement ledge 1.4 metres above ground level. Excavated by A. Young between 1953 and 1955, the site revealed two distinct occupation phases spanning the 4th to 7th centuries AD. Finds included bone composite combs, ornamental bone pins, bone gaming dice, stone tools, querns, metal objects, and two distinct pottery traditions -- Dun Cuier ware and later plain coarse pottery associated with Gaelic settlement. The site is classified as broch-like rather than a true broch, as it lacks certain features such as an intra-mural stair.

card_description: The largest megalithic ensemble in the Balkans, built on a 470-metre hill from 5000 BC. A giant multi-story structure and monumental rock-cut architecture have been uncovered.
description: Perperikon is the largest megalithic ensemble in the Balkans, situated on a 470m rocky hill in the Eastern Rhodope Mountains near Kardzhali, Bulgaria. Occupation traces date to the 6th millennium BC, with intensive rock-carved construction during the Bronze Age (18th-12th centuries BC). The site features a labyrinthine palace of over 50 rock-hewn halls, corridors, and staircases, plus a ritual chamber with a 2m-diameter altar. Scholars identify it as the legendary Oracle of Dionysus, where priestesses allegedly prophesied for Alexander the Great. Romans fortified it in the 1st century BC, Christians built basilicas in the 5th century, and it was abandoned after the Ottoman invasion of 1362.

description: Portus Adurni is a 3rd-century Roman Saxon Shore fort at the north end of Portsmouth Harbour, widely regarded as the best-preserved Roman fort north of the Alps. Likely built by Carausius c. 285-290 AD to defend against Saxon raiders, the fort was later converted into Portchester Castle following the Norman Conquest, and Professor Barry Cunliffe's excavations (1961-1979) transformed understanding of the site.

description: The Temple of Jupiter is a temple in Split, Croatia dedicated to the Ancient Roman god Jupiter [1]. Since the Emperor unexpectedly abdicated the throne in 305 and arrived at the palace from Nicomedia earlier, finishing work on the construction of the Palace was stopped so parts of the Temple remained unfinished [1].
